item.title: ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp
item.description:
Chrome DevTools for coding agents

https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/agents

Chrome DevTools for agents

Chrome DevTools for agents (chrome-devtools-mcp) lets your coding agent (such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor or Copilot) control and inspect a live Chrome browser. It is available as a Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server and as a CLI. Both give your AI coding assistant access to the full power of Chrome DevTools for reliable automation, in-depth debugging, and performance analysis.

Tool reference | CLI | Skills | Changelog | Contributing | Troubleshooting | Design Principles

Key features

  • Get performance insights: Uses Chrome DevTools to record traces and extract actionable performance insights.
  • Advanced browser debugging: Analyze network requests, take screenshots and check browser console messages (with source-mapped stack traces).
  • Reliable automation. Uses puppeteer to automate actions in Chrome and automatically wait for action results.

Disclaimers

chrome-devtools-mcp exposes content of the browser instance to the MCP clients allowing them to inspect, debug, and modify any data in the browser or DevTools. Avoid sharing sensitive or personal information that you don't want to share with MCP clients.

chrome-devtools-mcp officially supports Google Chrome and Chrome for Testing only. Other Chromium-based browsers may work, but this is not guaranteed, and you may encounter unexpected behavior. Use at your own discretion. We are committed to providing fixes and support for the latest version of Extended Stable Chrome.

Performance tools may send trace URLs to the Google CrUX API to fetch real-user experience data. This helps provide a holistic performance picture by presenting field data alongside lab data. This data is collected by the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX). To disable this, run with the --no-performance-crux flag.

Usage statistics

Google collects usage statistics (such as tool invocation success rates, latency, and environment information) to improve the reliability and performance of Chrome DevTools MCP.

Data collection is enabled by default. You can opt-out by passing the --no-usage-statistics flag when starting the server:

"args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest", "--no-usage-statistics"]

Google handles this data in accordance with the Google Privacy Policy.

Google's collection of usage statistics for Chrome DevTools MCP is independent from the Chrome browser's usage statistics. Opting out of Chrome metrics does not automatically opt you out of this tool, and vice-versa.

Collection is disabled if CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_USAGE_STATISTICS or CI env variables are set.

Update checks

By default, the server periodically checks the npm registry for updates and logs a notification when a newer version is available. You can disable these update checks by setting the CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_UPDATE_CHECKS environment variable.

Requirements

  • Node.js LTS version.
  • Chrome current stable version or newer.
  • npm

Getting started

Add the following config to your MCP client:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}

Note

Using chrome-devtools-mcp@latest ensures that your MCP client will always use the latest version of the Chrome DevTools MCP server.

MCP Client configuration

For setup instructions specific to your editor or agent (e.g. Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code), please see our Client Configurations Guide.

Your first prompt

Enter the following prompt in your MCP Client to check if everything is working:

Check the performance of https://developers.chrome.com

Your MCP client should open the browser and record a performance trace.

Note

The MCP server will start the browser automatically once the MCP client uses a tool that requires a running browser instance. Connecting to the Chrome DevTools MCP server on its own will not automatically start the browser.

CLI

The package also includes the chrome-devtools CLI. Use it to control the browser from your terminal without MCP:

npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
chrome-devtools navigate_page 1 --url "https://developers.chrome.com"
chrome-devtools take_screenshot 1 --filePath screenshot.png
chrome-devtools stop

See the CLI guide for all commands and options.

Skills

The package includes skills that teach your agent how to use Chrome DevTools:

Skill Use it to
chrome-devtools Debug and automate pages with the MCP tools.
chrome-devtools-cli Run the CLI and write shell scripts with it.
a11y-debugging Audit and fix accessibility issues.
cookie-debugging Debug cookies, sessions, and authentication.
debug-optimize-lcp Debug and improve Largest Contentful Paint.
memory-leak-debugging Find and fix memory leaks.
troubleshooting Fix connection problems between MCP and Chrome.

Install skills as a plugin

A plugin installs the MCP server and all skills, including the CLI skill:

  • Claude Code: Run /plugin marketplace add ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp, then /plugin install chrome-devtools-mcp@chrome-devtools-plugins.
  • Copilot / VS Code: Run Chat: Install Plugin From Source and enter ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp.
  • Gemini CLI: Run gemini extensions install --auto-update https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp.

See the Client Configurations Guide for more information.

Install skills manually

If your agent does not support plugins, copy the skill folders into the skills directory of your agent. The npm package contains the skills:

npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
# Example for Claude Code. Use the skills directory of your agent.
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/

Important

The chrome-devtools-cli skill requires the CLI. Install the package globally before you use the skill.

Keep skills up to date

Skills describe the tools of a specific version. Update the skills each time you update the MCP server or the CLI. Outdated skills can tell your agent to use tools or parameters that changed.

  • Plugins: Use the update command of the plugin manager of your agent. The Gemini CLI command above enables automatic updates with --auto-update.
  • Manual installs: Update the package, then copy the skill folders again:
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/

Tools

If you run into any issues, checkout our troubleshooting guide. See the full Tool Reference for a complete list of all supported MCP capabilities.

Configuration

Find the complete list of server parameters (e.g., --headless, --isolated, --slim) and how to configure WebSocket connections in the Configuration Guide.

For basic browser tasks only, the --slim flag exposes a reduced set of tools. See the Slim tool reference.

Advanced Usage

For advanced features such as handling concurrent sessions, persistent user data directories, using a custom or non-standard browser path (--executablePath), connecting to a running Chrome instance instead of starting a new one, or debugging on Android, see our Advanced Usage Guide.

Integrating as a browser subagent

If you are developing agentic tooling and want to provide an integrated browser subagent as part of your product, we recommend building on top of Chrome DevTools for agents.

For a reference implementation, see the Gemini CLI browser agent documentation.

item.title: ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui
item.description:
AG-UI: the Agent-User Interaction Protocol. Bring Agents into Frontend Applications.

https://ag-ui.com

The open protocol that connects any agent to any app.

Docs · Examples · Spec · Discord


AG-UI is an open, lightweight, event-based protocol that standardizes how AI agents connect to user-facing applications.

Agents don't fit the request/response model. They stream tokens, call tools mid-response, update shared state, pause for a human, and spawn subagents, and every framework does it differently. AG-UI replaces that custom wiring with one bi-directional event stream: the agent emits typed events, and any client can render them, no matter which framework built the agent. The same agent can power a web app, a mobile app, a terminal, or Slack.

Important

AG-UI 1.0 is here. The protocol now has a stable, frozen specification backed by a JSON Schema, and the TypeScript, Python, and .NET SDKs are generated from it. 1.0 is backwards compatible in both directions: 0.x agents work with 1.0 clients and vice versa. What changed → · Migration guide →

Quick start

Start a new app. The CLI scaffolds a frontend (CopilotKit on Next.js, or a terminal client) wired to the agent framework you pick:

npx create-ag-ui-app@latest

Then follow the printed next steps. The generated templates call OpenAI, so set your key before npm run dev:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
Or speak the protocol directly: a 30-line agent server and client

An AG-UI agent is any HTTP endpoint that accepts a RunAgentInput and streams events back. No API keys needed for this one.

1. The agent (Python). Requires Python 3.9+.

pip install ag-ui-protocol fastapi uvicorn

# server.py
import uuid

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from ag_ui.core import (
    PROTOCOL_VERSION,
    RunAgentInput,
    RunStartedEvent,
    RunFinishedEvent,
    TextMessageStartEvent,
    TextMessageContentEvent,
    TextMessageEndEvent,
)
from ag_ui.encoder import EventEncoder

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/")
async def run_agent(input_data: RunAgentInput, request: Request):
    encoder = EventEncoder(accept=request.headers.get("accept"))

    async def events():
        yield encoder.encode(RunStartedEvent(
            thread_id=input_data.thread_id,
            run_id=input_data.run_id,
            protocol_version=PROTOCOL_VERSION,
        ))
        message_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
        yield encoder.encode(TextMessageStartEvent(message_id=message_id, role="assistant"))
        for chunk in ["Hello ", "from ", "AG-UI!"]:
            yield encoder.encode(TextMessageContentEvent(message_id=message_id, delta=chunk))
        yield encoder.encode(TextMessageEndEvent(message_id=message_id))
        yield encoder.encode(RunFinishedEvent(thread_id=input_data.thread_id, run_id=input_data.run_id))

    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type=encoder.get_content_type())

uvicorn server:app --port 8000

2. The client (TypeScript). In a second terminal, in a new folder. Requires Node.js 20+.

npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm install @ag-ui/client tsx

// client.ts
import { HttpAgent } from "@ag-ui/client";

const agent = new HttpAgent({ url: "http://localhost:8000/" });

agent.addMessage({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), role: "user", content: "Hi there!" });

await agent.runAgent({}, {
  onRunStartedEvent: ({ event }) => console.log(`run started (AG-UI ${event.protocolVersion})`),
  onTextMessageContentEvent: ({ event }) => { process.stdout.write(event.delta); },
  onRunFinishedEvent: () => console.log("\nrun finished"),
});

npx tsx client.ts

Where AG-UI fits

AG-UI is one of three open, complementary agentic protocols. MCP gives agents tools and context, A2A lets agents work with other agents, and AG-UI brings agents to users. A single agent often uses all three, and AG-UI can front agents that speak MCP or A2A. Read more →

Note

AG-UI or A2UI? They work together. A2UI, MCP Apps, and Open-JSON-UI are generative UI specs: they describe what UI an agent wants to show. AG-UI is the runtime protocol that carries those payloads, along with everything else, between the agent and the app. Learn more →

Integrations

How it works

Your app starts a run by sending the agent a single RunAgentInput: the conversation, the tools the frontend offers, shared state, and context. The agent answers with a stream of typed events from eight families: run lifecycle, text messages, tool calls, state, reasoning, activity, subagents, and custom events (full list). Only the run lifecycle is required, so a minimal agent emits a handful of events and grows from there.

AG-UI is transport-agnostic. The spec defines HTTP + SSE and a binary HTTP + Protobuf binding, and middleware can adapt events from any source. Read the architecture overview for the full picture.

item.title: meta/astryx
item.description:
An open source design system that's fully customizable and agent ready

http://astryx.atmeta.com

Astryx

An open source design system that's fully customizable and built for how we build now:
by people and the agents working alongside them.

Currently in Beta · Built on React 19+ and StyleX

Docs · Storybook · Sandbox · Contributing · Discord

Overview

Astryx is an open source design system that grew inside Meta over the last eight years, where it became the most-used and largest design system in the company — powering 13,000+ apps and shaped by the engineers, designers, and product teams who depend on it every day.

It ships 150+ accessible components, brand-level theming, dark mode, ready-to-ship templates, and a CLI as one cohesive system. You import pre-built CSS and use typed React components — no build plugin, no styling library to adopt — and both people and AI assistants build with the same tooling.

What makes Astryx different:

  • Open internals. Components are built to be composed at any level, not locked behind a closed top-level API. The building blocks you'd reach for are exported directly, and when you need to go deeper, swizzle ejects a component's full source into your project to own.
  • No styling lock-in. Astryx authors its styles with StyleX, but that's invisible to consumers. Override with className using Tailwind, CSS modules, or plain CSS — whatever your project already uses.
  • Customize without wrapping. A theme is a set of CSS custom property overrides, so a designer can make Astryx unmistakably theirs without forking or wrapping component source.
  • Built for people and agents. The API, docs, and CLI are designed together so a person and an AI assistant build the same way, from the same reference.

Getting Started

Astryx requires React 19 or later (react and react-dom are peer dependencies of @astryxdesign/core).

Install Astryx, a theme, and its peer dependencies:

# npm
npm install @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
npm install -D @astryxdesign/cli

# pnpm
pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
pnpm add -D @astryxdesign/cli

# yarn
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli

Then finish setup with init, once, before you write UI. It asks no questions, prints the getting-started steps (styles, theme), and saves the Astryx guide to AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md so you and your agents build with Astryx instead of guessing:

npx @astryxdesign/cli init   # or: pnpm exec astryx init / yarn astryx init

You can also install the CLI once for your computer, so astryx works in any folder and every coding agent knows Astryx; in a project, it still runs that project's own version:

npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli

Project install, global install, or both? astryx docs global/project-global-or-both compares them (both is recommended), and astryx docs global explains how global mode works.

The simplest setup is a few CSS imports plus a theme provider — no build plugin, no PostCSS or Babel config. See the @astryxdesign/core README for the full guide (Next.js, Tailwind, Vite, and CDN).

For reliable CLI access, add a script to your package.json:

"scripts": {
  "astryx": "node node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/clients/cli/bin/astryx.mjs"
}

Then use it as npm run astryx -- component --list. This avoids path errors when AI assistants or new developers invoke the CLI directly.

Packages

Package Description README
@astryxdesign/core Components, theme system, and utilities README
@astryxdesign/cli CLI tooling: component docs, templates, scaffolding, themes, and codemods README
@astryxdesign/build Build plugins for StyleX source builds README
@astryxdesign/theme-* Seven ready-made, fully customizable themes (neutral, butter, chocolate, matcha, stone, gothic, y2k) README

@astryxdesign/lab (experimental components) is used internally for Storybook and the sandbox and is not published to npm. @astryxdesign/vega (Vega/Vega-Lite chart wrapper) and @astryxdesign/charts (chart components) are published to npm only under the @canary dist-tag — there is no stable release yet.

Principles

These are the promises Astryx makes to the people building on it.

  • Guidance over enforcement. Components give you capability rather than guardrails that fight you. Design opinions live in docs and examples — if you pass a value, the component renders it.
  • Strong, documented conventions. Every component follows the same naming, prop, and composition rules, and every one is thoroughly documented — so once you've learned a few, the rest feel familiar, and both people and AI can predict how an unfamiliar component behaves.
  • One system for humans and AI. The API, conventions, docs, and CLI are designed together so people and AI assistants build the same way. Every change that made Astryx easier for AI made it easier for people too.
  • Earned by measurement. We test conventions rather than assert them, hold the results loosely, and revisit them when a new situation proves them wrong.

Architecture

Foundations

The building blocks for visually cohesive and accessible interfaces: typography, color, layout, and accessibility.

Components

A library of 150+ reusable UI building blocks with full TypeScript support.

Patterns

Battle-tested design solutions for common interactions and workflows: table pages, detail page layouts, form wizards, navigation patterns, data entry flows.

Project Structure

Directory Purpose
apps/ Example apps, the docsite, and Storybook
packages/ Published packages: core, cli, build, themes
internal/ Internal tooling: test utilities, eslint plugin, vibe tests

Contributing

We welcome contributions! See CONTRIBUTING.md for the full guide.

Questions, or want a hand with a PR? Come find us in Discord.

Our conventions and review rubrics live in the Contributing wiki — including API Conventions, Design Conventions, the Component Lifecycle, the Contributing Templates, and the Blog Review Rubric. Read the relevant rubric before opening a PR.

Quick start for contributors: this repo uses Node 22+ on an active LTS line and pnpm 11. Install pnpm directly, or enable Corepack once so the pinned pnpm version installs automatically:

corepack enable
pnpm install

If corepack is missing, install pnpm directly or install Corepack manually; see the troubleshooting notes in CONTRIBUTING.md.

The Theme Showcase DOM tests use the root ui project for shared DOM and StyleX test setup. Run pnpm exec vitest run --project ui apps/docsite/src/__tests__/theme-showcase/ from the repository root.

License

Build your own AI office with Univer Office SDK. Bring editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing into your product for people and AI agents. Built on an extensible open-source core.

https://univer.ai

Build your own AI office with Univer Office SDK.

Start with open-source Sheets and Docs, then connect your own application or agent.

🚀 Quick start · 💼 Workspace · 📚 Documentation · ⚖️ Feature comparison · 🌐 Website · 🎮 Showcase · 🔧 API Reference · 📝 Blog

English · Français · Deutsch · Español · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어

Table of contents
  • 💡 What is Univer?
    • Open-source capabilities
  • 🚀 Build on the open-source foundation
    • Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor
    • Connect your application to editable content
  • 🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture
    • Give custom features clear boundaries
    • Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo
    • Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events
  • 🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK
    • Scope and licensing
  • 🌐 Application patterns and ecosystem
    • Univer Workspace: an Office SDK reference application
    • CLI, agent integrations, and developer skills
  • 📚 Documentation and contributing
    • Runtime compatibility
  • 💬 Community
  • 🔒 Security
  • ❤️ Sponsors

💡 What is Univer?

Univer is an Office SDK for building Office applications inside your own product. It provides Office editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing for people and existing agents, using your data and permissions. The product family covers spreadsheets, documents, presentations, relational tables, canvases, and PDFs.

Univer Office SDK has three parts:

  • Web SDK is the foundation: content models, editing, rendering, formula calculation, and Facade APIs (application-facing APIs). Compose its plugins into an embedded editor or your own Office application, and reuse the content models, commands, and calculation for Headless processing without an interactive editor.
  • Server SDK adds backend services for real-time collaboration, edit history, and Office file import and export.
  • AI SDK connects Office capabilities to existing agents and workflows, with content tools, execution, and review integrations.

This repository provides the Web SDK's core architecture and engine implementations under Apache-2.0: content models and snapshot formats, plugin and dependency management, the command system, formula and rendering engines, Facade APIs, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs editing capabilities. Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and commercial AI SDK extensions are distributed and licensed separately.

Agents can use the same open-source APIs; your application supplies the model and tool orchestration. The quotation example demonstrates editing, calculation, and saving without an AI SDK dependency.

Open-source capabilities

Area Selected capabilities
Sheets · Editing and layout Cell styles, merged cells, in-cell rich text, freeze panes, floating images, and undo/redo.
Sheets · Data and calculation Formulas, defined names, filtering, sorting, data validation, conditional formatting, hyperlinks, comments, and find and replace.
Docs Rich-text editing, paragraph formatting, lists, hyperlinks, comments, and drawing integration.

Features are composed through plugins and presets; the quick start uses only the Sheets Core preset. Images use the corresponding drawing plugins. See the feature comparison for detailed open-source and commercial coverage.

The demos below showcase the wider Univer Office SDK, including commercial capabilities. They show more than the default open-source setup; see open source and commercial extensions for scope.

🚀 Build on the open-source foundation

Your goal Use the open-source foundation Start here
Embed Sheets or Docs Add an editable Office surface to your application or agent product, and connect your data through Facade APIs. Quick start
Process content without an editor Reuse content plugins, models, commands, and calculation in Node.js for editing, snapshots, and automated tasks. Headless guide
Develop custom features or editors Reuse the engines, UI components, plugin boundaries, dependency injection, and command/undo systems. Follow existing features to extend Sheets and Docs or develop your own editors. Open-source architecture

Coordinate edits and undo/redo across features. Inserting a row inside a filter range changes both the base content and the filter range; undo needs to restore both. Each feature supplies its own changes and undo data, and the command composes their execution and history. The architecture walkthrough explains how to extend these editing workflows.

Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor

In a browser application using a bundler such as Vite:

pnpm add @univerjs/presets @univerjs/preset-sheets-core

Create the container before initializing Univer:

<div id="app" style="height: 100vh"></div>

import { UniverSheetsCorePreset } from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core'
import UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/locales/en-US'
import { createUniver, LocaleType, mergeLocales } from '@univerjs/presets'
import '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/lib/index.css'

const { univerAPI } = createUniver({
  locale: LocaleType.EN_US,
  locales: {
    [LocaleType.EN_US]: mergeLocales(UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS),
  },
  presets: [
    UniverSheetsCorePreset({
      container: 'app',
    }),
  ],
})

univerAPI.createWorkbook({})

Your page now contains a spreadsheet editor. Use the returned univerAPI to work with its content. This example uses open-source packages and needs no commercial Univer license or Server SDK.

For component frameworks, retain the univer instance returned by createUniver and call univer.dispose() when the component unmounts. See the lifecycle guide.

Presets compose plugins and register their Facade APIs. For manual control, see the Plugin Mode example below. The installation guide covers both modes, peer dependencies, and framework integrations.

Keep coordinated @univerjs/* packages on the same version. Commercial packages must use the matching release line; independently released packages such as icons follow their declared compatibility. See the API Stability Policy.

Connect your application to editable content

Facade APIs are the application-facing interface to workbooks, worksheets, and ranges. Continue from the quick start to populate a quotation, update a quantity from application code, and read the recalculated total:

// Wait for formula controllers before editing a newly created workbook.
await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
  if (univerAPI.getCurrentLifecycleStage() >= univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) {
    resolve()
    return
  }
  const listener = univerAPI.addEvent(univerAPI.Event.LifeCycleChanged, ({ stage }) => {
    if (stage === univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) {
      listener.dispose()
      resolve()
    }
  })
})

const workbook = univerAPI.getActiveWorkbook()!
const sheet = workbook.getActiveSheet()

sheet.getRange('A1:D4').setValues([
  ['Item', 'Quantity', 'Unit price', 'Amount'],
  ['Seats', 2, 25, '=B2*C2'],
  ['Support', 1, 100, '=B3*C3'],
  ['Total', '', '', '=SUM(D2:D3)'],
])

// An application control or agent can make the same edit.
sheet.getRange('B2').setValue(4)

univerAPI.getFormula().onCalculationResultApplied().then(() => {
  console.log(sheet.getRange('D4').getValue()) // 200
  localStorage.setItem('quotation', JSON.stringify(workbook.save()))
}).catch(console.error)

The editor and your application operate on the same workbook; formula changes are recalculated automatically. workbook.save() returns a JSON snapshot containing the workbook and its registered plugin data. Your application owns persistence; this example uses browser storage. On a later page load, after initialization, restore the snapshot instead of creating a blank workbook:

const saved = localStorage.getItem('quotation')
if (saved) {
  univerAPI.createWorkbook(JSON.parse(saved))
}

This workflow uses only open-source packages. Snapshot persistence is separate from XLSX import and export, which uses the separately distributed file-conversion capabilities. Use public Facade APIs for application integration; the source links below explain internal implementation and extension points. See the API Stability Policy before depending on an extension point.

Advanced: compose plugins manually (Plugin Mode)

Use Plugin Mode when you need precise control over plugin selection, dependencies, or loading. The preset above handles this composition for you.

This alternative initialization uses the same app container and the Sheets Core preset's browser plugin stack without a Worker. Use it instead of the preset initialization, then run the same quotation example with the returned univerAPI.

pnpm add @univerjs/core @univerjs/design @univerjs/docs @univerjs/docs-ui \
  @univerjs/engine-formula @univerjs/engine-render @univerjs/network \
  @univerjs/sheets @univerjs/sheets-ui @univerjs/sheets-formula \
  @univerjs/sheets-formula-ui @univerjs/sheets-numfmt \
  @univerjs/sheets-numfmt-ui @univerjs/ui

import { LocaleType, mergeLocales, Univer } from '@univerjs/core'
import { FUniver } from '@univerjs/core/facade'
import DesignEnUS from '@univerjs/design/locale/en-US'
import { UniverDocsPlugin } from '@univerjs/docs'
import { UniverDocsUIPlugin } from '@univerjs/docs-ui'
import DocsUIEnUS from '@univerjs/docs-ui/locale/en-US'
import { UniverFormulaEnginePlugin } from '@univerjs/engine-formula'
import FormulaEnUS from '@univerjs/engine-formula/locale/en-US'
import { UniverRenderEnginePlugin } from '@univerjs/engine-render'

const univer = new Univer({
  locale: LocaleType.EN_US,
  locales: {
    [LocaleType.EN_US]: mergeLocales(
      DesignEnUS,
      DocsUIEnUS,
      FormulaEnUS,

univer.registerPlugin(UniverDocsUIPlugin)
univer.registerPlugin(UniverFormulaEnginePlugin)

  onlyRegisterFormulaRelatedMutations: false,
})

})

univer.registerPlugin(UniverSheetsNumfmtUIPlugin)

const univerAPI = FUniver.newAPI(univer)

The Docs plugins support spreadsheet rich-text editing. When adding a feature, include its corresponding Facade extensions, locale bundles, and UI styles. Dispose univer when its container is unmounted.

🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture

Give custom features clear boundaries

Univer organizes content logic and UI interaction in separate plugins. Feature plugins manage rules and content changes; UI plugins provide the interface and user interactions. For example, sheets-filter manages filter ranges and rules, while sheets-filter-ui provides panels, menus, and shortcuts.

Arrows mean “contains.” Both plugins can contain Controllers and Services: logic Controllers coordinate content changes and related features; UI Controllers connect menus, shortcuts, and interactions, with UI Services managing panel state. These responsibilities give new features a consistent structure to implement and test.

The UI foundation follows the same division. @univerjs/design supplies shared components and styles, @univerjs/ui provides workbench services such as menus, shortcuts, panels, and component registration, and @univerjs/icons supplies icons. A feature registers its components and icons, contributes menus, and attaches its rendering through these extension points. Teams can add a panel or toolbar feature while reusing the application's UI infrastructure. See the UI overview and the filter plugin's component and icon registration.

Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo

For example, when rows are inserted inside a filter range, the filter plugin supplies the corresponding range change and its undo data. The row command composes the base edit and participating feature changes, executes them, and records their undo/redo information together. The row insertion feature can use the shared extension mechanism while the filter plugin owns its range-update rules.

The command system distinguishes three kinds of action:

  • Command orchestrates a business action and the changes it requires.
  • Mutation changes content saved in a snapshot, with serializable parameters.
  • Operation changes transient state, such as an open panel or the scroll position.

A shared structure for undo/redo. For an undoable edit, the feature implementation supplies the forward mutations and corresponding inverse mutations, and the Command records them through IUndoRedoService. When one action affects several features, the Command can combine their changes and undo data in a single undo/redo record, so the user can undo and redo the complete action. See extending commands.

Features still need to cooperate. Interceptors and reference-range handlers give that cooperation a defined place. At supported extension points, plugins contribute checks or related mutations; interceptor priorities control ordering where the API defines it.

These boundaries support a practical testing strategy: test models and services independently, replace external dependencies through DI, and add regression cases for combined actions and undo/redo. The filter controller tests exercise row and column changes and their effect on filtering.

Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events

The repository includes the content models, formula engine, and Canvas rendering and layout engine behind the editors. They are shared building blocks: spreadsheet rich text, for example, reuses document layout and rendering. Custom features can build on these engines instead of implementing a separate content stack. Read about the formula engine architecture and rendering engine architecture.

Browser editors, Node.js Headless tasks, and appropriately composed Workers can reuse the corresponding content plugins, models, commands, and calculation. See Headless Univer and the isomorphic architecture.

ICommandService exposes execution callbacks so plugins can observe commands before and after execution. Facade APIs wrap the underlying capabilities in application objects such as FWorkbook, FWorksheet, and FRange.

Each plugin contributes its own Facade extensions, typed events through univerAPI.Event, and enums through univerAPI.Enum. Application code can discover event names and constants from one entry point instead of importing private services or repeating strings. For example, BeforeCommandExecute can inspect and cancel an execution; CommandExecuted reports executions to listeners. Listeners return disposables, and cancellation applies where the event supports it.

Facade extensions stay with their feature packages, so a content API does not have to pull in unrelated UI APIs. See the Facade design, command callbacks and event bridge, and Enum entry point.

The repository provides working feature implementations and patterns for extending them. Read the filter implementation walkthrough for a complete example, or the API Stability Policy before depending on an extension point.

🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK

When you want more ready-to-integrate capabilities, compose the corresponding Univer Office SDK modules: additional content types, advanced editing plugins, collaboration, file conversion, and agent tooling. They extend the same content models, plugin architecture, command system, and Facade design introduced above, so you can build on your existing integration.

Commercial Web SDK plugins Follow the core's Plugin, dependency injection, Command/Mutation, and Facade extension patterns. Add charts, shapes, pivot tables, SmartArt, and other features for the corresponding content types.
Server SDK Extends the same content models and mutation conventions with real-time collaboration, revision history, and Office file conversion. Integrates with your application's identity, permissions, and storage.
AI SDK extensions Reuse Web SDK Headless and Facade capabilities to provide composable Node.js APIs and CLI building blocks for agents to inspect, edit, and check content, with collaboration and Worktree review integrations.

  • This repository: Apache-2.0 packages that can be used in commercial applications under that license, including the open-source Headless content capabilities.
  • Commercial extensions: Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and AI SDK capabilities beyond the open-source foundation are distributed and licensed separately. Freemium evaluation includes watermarks and feature limits.
  • Reference applications: Open-source applications such as Univer Workspace have their own source licenses. Their SDK dependencies retain their respective licenses.

See the feature comparison, including its Open source only filter, for detailed coverage and plans and licensing for commercial options.

How shared content models connect editing, collaboration, and files

These capabilities operate on serializable Unit snapshots, including Sheets' IWorkbookData, Docs' IDocumentData, Slides' ISlideData, and canvases' IBoardData (called Boards in the API). These types come from core and the respective product packages; current Slides and Boards capabilities are separately distributed commercial products. The shared Unit conventions let browser editors, backend services, and agents work with the same content.

Commands orchestrate edits; Mutations describe content changes. Collaboration packages those mutations into changesets, applies operational transformation (OT) to concurrent changes, and manages confirmed revisions and snapshots. History can reconstruct a revision from a snapshot and subsequent changesets. Read the collaboration design and Collaboration SDK overview.

Exchange maps Office file structures to and from Univer content snapshots. For OOXML formats such as XLSX, DOCX, and PPTX, it parses the file into the corresponding Sheet, Doc, or Slide data and generates the file representation on export. The converted content can enter the same editing, calculation, collaboration, and agent workflows. See Office file import and export.

How AI SDK gives agents the same content capabilities

AI SDK builds on the Web SDK's Headless content models, commands, calculation, and Facade APIs. It exposes structured TypeScript APIs and optional Commander presets that applications can compose into their own Office CLI or agent tools.

  • Understand, discover, and edit. Inspection returns structured content. API Reference helps the agent find Facade symbols and signatures shipped with its SDK. Facade execution distinguishes read and write modes, captures mutations, and works with explicit synchronization and commit results. See content operations.
  • Check the rendered result. A browser Render Runtime reuses Web SDK rendering for screenshots. Slide layout lint adds structured findings for issues such as off-page or overlapping text, giving the agent evidence for another editing pass. See visual inspection.
  • Edit drafts for human review. With the corresponding collaboration and Web capabilities, agents can edit and verify an isolated Worktree draft over several rounds, then hand it to a person to review, merge, or reopen. The workflow uses the same snapshots, mutations, and revision conventions. See Worktree.

For repeated calls, optional Worker pools and a daemon reuse loaded content instances and reduce repeated initialization. Your application owns the root CLI, targets, authorization, and output. Explore the AI SDK package catalog to select the required capabilities.

For a complete application reference, start with Univer Workspace. It shows how to compose Univer Office SDK editors, collaboration, file capabilities, existing agents, and human review into a self-hostable workspace. item.title: a2ui-project/a2ui
item.description:
Open-source generative UI framework: agents stream layout data, and apps render it with native components in React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose.

https://a2ui.org/

A2UI

Build delightful, fast, reliable agentic experiences

A2UI (Agent-to-User Interface) is an open-source generative UI framework, complete with a protocol optimized for streaming dynamic user interfaces at low latency, native renderers for web and mobile frameworks, and agent SDKs in several popular languages. With A2UI, your agents can communicate with your users using natively rendered widgets, in addition to text.

Examples of UI compositions that A2UI can express.

Quick links

  • Main website.
  • Try it in your browser using A2UI Composer.
  • Supported renderers.
  • Supported agents.
  • Protocol specification.

Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) and decision models (e.g. Jev) excel at creating text and code and at making fast decisions on top of raw structured data (e.g. JSON). A2UI gives these models a specialized vocabulary for expressing user interfaces.

A2UI expresses UI using data, not code. A schema for the data exchanged between the agent and the renderer enforces strict capability boundaries for the agent, keeping agent-generated experiences safe and aligned with the business requirements of your application. A core library, a native framework adapter, and a catalog of components provide access to native components and form the building blocks that the agent composes into a final user experience, making the result expressive and high-performance.

When to use A2UI

Use A2UI when any of the following apply to your application:

  • Parts of your application are agent- and/or server-driven. By design, A2UI supports remote rendering.
  • You want the UI to be composed dynamically, tailored to the user's immediate need. Instead of making your users navigate through multiple screens to solve their problems, have the agent build the right flow of UI that guides users directly to solutions.
  • You need the highest performance and visual fidelity. A2UI renders UI using the framework of your choice, typically one that the host app itself is written in. WebViews or HTML are not required.
  • The same agent streams UI to multiple platforms or frameworks, such as Flutter, React, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose. A2UI helps keep the user experience compatible and consistent across all screens.
  • The agent is remote, third-party, or operates across a trust boundary. For example, the agent must not be able to handle certain kinds of data (credit card/account numbers, PII, financial data). A2UI helps enforce the trust boundary and protect your app's critical functionality from hallucinations using a strict schema, and by expressing UI using validated data rather than executable code.

A2UI core philosophy

We develop A2UI under the guidance of the following core principles:

  • Security first: The app developer controls what the agent can and cannot do in the app. A2UI provides a framework for specifying and enforcing the necessary guardrails, such as expressing UI as data, validating inputs and outputs against a schema, and disallowing arbitrary executable code. Every capability granted to the agent is either a safe standard capability built into the framework, or a capability explicitly granted by the app developer.
  • Model-friendly and server-driven: The A2UI protocol is designed to be efficiently generated by language and decision models and transported over the network, and to support progressive rendering (or "streaming") for a responsive user experience. An agent can adapt the UI based on where the user takes the conversation. A2UI supports swappable inference formats, so you can tailor inference to specific models and use cases.
  • Native rendering and portability: A2UI renders UI using the framework native to your app, with renderers for many major UI frameworks. No need to change frameworks unless required for other reasons.

Architecture

A2UI's architecture is made of multiple layers spanning the full stack that connects the agent to the application:

  1. Inference: An agent (typically backed by a language or a decision model) instructed by an A2UI skill (created using an A2UI Agent SDK) generates the description of UI and data using an appropriate inference format (e.g. A2UI Express, or a decision tree).
  2. Transport: An A2UI Agent SDK, embedded in a larger agent architecture, parses and validates the model's output, expands macros, and converts the UI to the wire-stable A2UI Transport protocol messages, which are sent to the renderer.
  3. Rendering: A renderer is made of an A2UI Core library (e.g. the @a2ui/web_core npm package, or a2ui_core Dart package), a UI framework adapter (e.g. @a2ui/react React adapter, or a2ui_flutter Flutter adapter), and a widget catalog. The core library parses the incoming messages and creates a framework-agnostic in-memory representation of the UI and data. The framework adapter maps the in-memory representation to concrete framework-specific UI widgets. The widget catalog provides access to the widgets the agent is allowed to compose.

Getting started

Pick the path that matches where you want to start:

Path What you get Time
🍜 Quickstart A full-stack A2UI app with a backend and frontend. Learn A2UI end-to-end and customize to your use case. ~5 min
🎨 A2UI Composer Generate A2UI JSON from a visual editor and paste it into any agent prompt — no install required. ~1 min
🎬 A2UI Theater Step through pre-built A2UI streaming scenarios across Lit, React, and Angular renderers — no install required. ~1 min

Packages

These packages are developed in this repository. Packages marked "Not published yet" can be used from source.

Python

Package Description Version
a2ui-core Protocol messages, data model, data binding, expression evaluation, and catalog validation.
a2ui-agent-sdk Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI.
a2ui-a2a Connects the agent SDK to the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol.
a2ui-adk Connects the agent SDK to the Agent Development Kit (ADK).

TypeScript

Package Description Version
@a2ui/web_core Protocol messages, state management, expressions, and basic catalog shared by renderers and @a2ui/agent.
@a2ui/lit Lit (web components) renderer.
@a2ui/angular Angular renderer.
@a2ui/react React renderer.
@a2ui/markdown-it Markdown rendering with markdown-it and DOMPurify, shared by the web renderers.
@a2ui/agent Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI.
@a2ui/catalog-mcp MCP catalog: calls MCP tools and renders A2UI messages returned in tool results and UI resources.
@a2ui/catalog-vegachart VegaChart catalog: renders Vega and Vega-Lite chart specifications on A2UI surfaces. Not published yet

Dart and Flutter

Package Description Version
a2ui_core Protocol messages, data model, data binding, and expressions for renderers and agents.
a2ui_agent Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI.
a2ui_flutter Flutter renderer.
a2ui_cli Developer tool that generates typesafe component code from a catalog. GitHub Releases

Swift

The Swift libraries are distributed via Swift Package Manager from Package.swift at the root of this repository.

Package Description
A2UISwiftCore, BasicCatalog Message processor, data model, expression evaluation, and basic catalog definitions.
A2UISwiftUI, BasicCatalogSwiftUI SwiftUI renderer and basic catalog views.

Roadmap

  • Protocol v1.1: We are collecting requirements for the next iteration of the A2UI protocol.
  • Inference: Support for decision models (e.g. Jev).
  • Templates: A cross-framework templating engine and a set of standard primitives for rendering reusable rich UI widgets.
  • Sandboxed logic: A way to securely attach logic to A2UI components.
  • Agent SDK: Skill generation, better diagnostics, and integrations with more agent frameworks.
  • Evals: A set of tools for evaluating generated UI quality.
  • MCP Apps: Embedding MCP Apps inside A2UI, and embedding A2UI experiences into MCP Apps.
  • CLI: Schema validation, codegen, local preview, and integration with coding agents.

Contribute

A2UI is an Apache 2.0 licensed project. We believe the future of UI is agentic, and we want to work with you to help build it.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for details on how to get started.

item.title: QwenLM/qwen-code
item.description:
An open-source AI coding agent that lives in your terminal.

https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/overview

The open-source AI coding agent for your terminal, editor, desktop, browser, and chat.

中文 | Deutsch | français | 日本語 | Русский | Português (Brasil) | 한국어

Qwen Code 1.0 Preview
Qwen Code 1.0 Preview brings together the agent harness capabilities of Qoder and Qwen Code in an open-source release.

Try Qwen Code 1.0 Preview · Documentation · 中文文档.

Why Qwen Code?

  • Agentic out of the box — Auto-Memory, Skills, SubAgents, and MCP work from the first session. Agent Teams, Agent Arena, and Dynamic Workflows are built in too — experimental or opt-in, as noted in Capabilities.
  • Open-source, inside and out — The framework and the Qwen models are open-source. They evolve together. No vendor lock-in.
  • Multi-protocol — Supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Qwen APIs. Any third-party provider or local model (Ollama / vLLM). Switch at runtime.
  • Beyond the terminal — IDE plugins, Desktop app, Web UI, SDKs, and chat integrations (Telegram / DingTalk / WeChat / WeCom / Feishu and more).

Tip

Qwen Code is actively iterating on itself — using its own agent and models to file issues, submit PRs, review code, and run tests. Powered by the community, driven by AI.

Installation

Looking for Qwen Code 1.0 Preview? Get started here. The instructions below are for the main version.

Linux / macOS:

curl -fsSL https://qwen-code-assets.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/installation/install-qwen-standalone.sh | bash

Windows:

irm https://qwen-code-assets.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/installation/install-qwen-standalone.ps1 | iex

Restart your terminal after installation to ensure environment variables take effect.

NPM / Homebrew

NPM (requires Node.js 22+):

npm install -g @qwen-code/qwen-code@latest

Homebrew (macOS / Linux):

brew install qwen-code

Quick Start

Open a terminal in your project and start Qwen Code:

cd /path/to/your-project
qwen

Inside the session, run /auth and choose Qwen Account with Subscription to sign in with your Plus or Pro subscription, or configure a provider with an API key. Then try:

Explain this repository and show me where to start.

See the Authentication Guide and Settings Reference for detailed setup.

See the terminal interface

How to Use Qwen Code

Choose the interface that fits your workflow:

Interface Get started
Terminal Run qwen in your project — see Quick Start.
Desktop Download Qwen Code Desktop for macOS, Windows, and Linux.
Web Run qwen serve --open to open the Web UI in your browser. (experimental)
Editor Set up VS Code, Zed, or JetBrains.
Chat Connect Telegram, DingTalk, WeChat, WeCom, Feishu, QQ Bot, Email, or GitHub, then run qwen channel start. See the Channels overview for webhook senders and plugin adapters.

For automation and custom integrations:

  • Headless — Run qwen -p "..." in scripts, CI/CD, or batch jobs.
  • SDKs — Build with TypeScript, Python, or Java.
  • Daemon — Run qwen serve to connect clients over HTTP + SSE (ACP). (experimental) Daemon guide.
  • Computer Use — Set up native MCP tools or Node REPL + SDK in Qwen Code, Claude Code, or Codex.
SDK example (Python) 
import asyncio

from qwen_code_sdk import is_sdk_result_message, query


async def main() -> None:
    result = query(
        "Summarize the repository layout.",
        {
            "cwd": "/path/to/project",
            "path_to_qwen_executable": "qwen",
        },
    )

    async for message in result:
        if is_sdk_result_message(message):
            print(message["result"])


asyncio.run(main())

Daemon Mode

Run Qwen Code as a long-lived service when you want browser, editor, SDK, and automation clients to share agent sessions without each starting a separate process. The daemon provides the built-in Web Shell and an HTTP + SSE API, supports multiple workspaces, and lets clients reconnect to active sessions.

Start it in the foreground and open the Web Shell:

qwen serve --open

The default address is http://127.0.0.1:4170. To run and manage it in the background instead:

qwen daemon start
qwen daemon status
qwen daemon logs -f
qwen daemon stop

By default, the daemon listens on loopback without bearer authentication; any local process that can reach it can use the full API, including code execution. On shared or untrusted hosts, set QWEN_SERVER_TOKEN and use --require-auth. See the Daemon guide for workspaces, authentication, remote access, and the API.

Capabilities

Qwen Code ships with a complete agent harness — multi-agent orchestration, persistent memory, and deep extensibility, all built in.

Agentic core

  • SubAgents — delegate focused subtasks to specialized agents with their own context and toolsets, in the foreground or background.
  • Agent Teams (experimental) — a leader coordinates teammates that share a task list and exchange messages, with read-only investigators and an optional single worktree writer.
  • Agent Arena (experimental) — run the same task on multiple models in isolated Git worktrees, compare solutions side by side, and merge the winner.
  • Dynamic Workflows (opt-in) — the model writes JavaScript workflows that orchestrate agents: parallel fan-out, verification passes, and resumable runs.
  • Goals — /goal keeps the session working across turns until an independent verifier accepts the outcome, within a token budget.
  • Scheduled tasks — /loop and cron tools re-run prompts on an interval or at a set time.

Memory, skills, and sessions

  • Auto-Memory — the agent writes its own notes and recalls them across sessions; your QWEN.md and AGENTS.md briefings load automatically.
  • Skills & Auto-Skills — built-in skills (/review, /batch, /bugfix…) work out of the box; /learn distills docs or code into new skills, the agent can generate skills on its own (opt-in), and /curator maintains the library.
  • Session management — resume past conversations with /resume, and browse, rename, or archive sessions.

Multimodal

  • Voice input — dictate prompts in the terminal or Web Shell with a configurable ASR model; the Web Shell inserts the transcript for review before sending.
  • Qwen Live (experimental) — realtime speech-to-speech conversations in the Web Shell that answer directly or hand tasks to the agent, with optional screen sharing.
  • Image generation — the built-in image_gen tool turns prompts into PNG artifacts using your configured image model.

Extensibility and control

  • Hooks — run your own scripts at lifecycle events: before and after tool calls, session start and end, and more.
  • MCP — connect any Model Context Protocol server to add tools, resources, and prompts.
  • LSP integration (experimental, opt-in) — native language-server support: go-to-definition, references, diagnostics, and code actions.
  • Computer Use & Browser Use — automate desktop applications and the browser through native MCP tools.
  • Plan Mode & approval modes — plan read-only before touching files, then choose per-call confirmation, auto-edit, classifier-driven Auto Mode, or YOLO.
  • Sandbox & Git worktrees — confine tool execution with built-in sandboxing and isolate wide-ranging edits in a temporary worktree.

Open and multi-platform

  • Open framework and models — the framework and the Qwen models are open source and evolve together.
  • Any provider — OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Qwen APIs, plus any third-party provider or local model (Ollama / vLLM). Switch at runtime.
  • Every interface — IDE plugins, desktop app, Web UI, IM channels, headless mode, SDKs, and daemon mode. See How to Use Qwen Code.

Qwen Code Evaluation

On SWE-bench Verified, seven Qwen Code versions scored 76.40%–77.80% on average using the same Qwen 3.7 Max model (500 tasks, three trials per version).

Full results and evaluation configuration →

Ecosystem

  • Qwen Code Desktop — Official desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux

  • AionUi — A modern GUI for command-line AI tools including Qwen Code

  • Gemini CLI Desktop — A cross-platform desktop/web/mobile UI for Qwen Code

  • qwen-audio-agent — Realtime full-duplex voice frontend for Qwen Code over ACP — talk hands-free with barge-in and a local wake word

item.title: openai/codex-security
item.description:
OpenAI's Codex Security CLI and TypeScript SDK for finding, validating, and fixing security vulnerabilities. npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@openai/codex-security

https://developers.openai.com/codex/security

Codex Security

Codex Security helps you find, investigate, and fix vulnerabilities in your code. Use its security workflows in Codex, or automate them with the @openai/codex-security CLI and TypeScript SDK.

  • In Codex: choose a security workflow.
  • In a terminal: install the CLI and scan your repository.
  • In automation: use the TypeScript SDK or GitHub Action.

Features

  • Scan repositories, selected paths, or Git changes. Deep scans repeat Standard scans and return their deduplicated findings.
  • Validate candidate findings, generate patches, and verify existing fixes.
  • Draft SECURITY.md policies and save threat models for later review.
  • Browse saved scans and findings, identify duplicates, assess severity against your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history.
  • Preview third-party scanner findings, save them locally, or publish supported reports to Codex Security Cloud. Scanner import guides.
  • Track findings in Linear, Jira, or GitHub, publish completed scans, or export SARIF, JSON, and CSV. Integration workflows.
  • Automate scans across repositories or project components, including in CI and containers.

Use in Codex

Open your repository in a Codex session with the Codex Security plugin enabled, then ask:

Run a Codex Security scan on this repository, focusing on authentication and authorization. Return the saved report, source evidence, and coverage limits.

A completed scan saves a report and findings. Read the report for source evidence and exclusions, then request a patch or ask Codex to verify an existing fix. See the agent workflow guide for setup, task selection, and recovery.

Quick start

Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+. Python 3.10 also requires tomli.

Install the CLI globally and sign in:

npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login

Run your first scan from the repository directory:

cs scan .

When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the REPORT path in the terminal. Run cs scans show from the same repository to find its latest completed scan again. See scan scope and follow-up work for how to interpret exclusions in the report.

cs and codex-security run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with another command, use codex-security. To skip the global install, or if npm reports an EEXIST conflict, use npx @openai/codex-security in place of cs for both login and scanning.

For CI, set OPENAI_API_KEY or CODEX_API_KEY in the scan process's environment. For a headless machine, see device or SSH login.

Scan options

Choose a scope and scan mode:

# Scan selected paths.
cs scan . --path src --path tests

# Exclude a directory from the scan.
cs scan . --exclude-path examples/

# Scan committed changes from a base revision to HEAD.
cs scan . --diff origin/main

# Run a deep scan of the repository.
cs scan . --mode deep

Use cs scan . --max-time 15 for an advisory 15-minute Standard investigation allowance. See investigation time for timing semantics and Deep Scan limits.

Use cs --help to browse commands, or cs scan --help for scan options, cost limits, and patching after a scan.

For an application spread across repositories, see review one system across repositories. Use bulk scans for independent repository reviews in one resumable campaign.

Scans use existing root and component SECURITY.md guidance. To write or revise it, see Generate SECURITY.md.

Some cybersecurity requests and protected findings require Trusted Access for Cyber. For accounts with Daybreak access, see Daybreak opt-in for the Codex toggle and Cyber access programs to select a program explicitly.

TypeScript SDK

Install the package locally in your TypeScript project:

npm install @openai/codex-security

Then import it:

import { CodexSecurity } from "@openai/codex-security";

const security = new CodexSecurity();

try {
  const result = await security.run("/path/to/repository");
  console.log(result.reportPath);
} finally {
  await security.close();
}

The SDK guide includes deep-scan configuration, validation, severity classification, owner suggestions, and result handling.

Linked Git worktrees share scan history and saved findings when they use the same Codex Security state directory. Keep CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR stable to retain that shared history and sign-in scope. See the scan history guide.

Read existing Cloud findings

When Codex Security Cloud is available to your account, the Security plugin's $cloud-findings skill can read findings, reports, recorded assignment and verification, and scan status in Codex desktop or the Codex CLI. Cloud is an optional connection; local scans work without it.

See Cloud connection setup and CLI reads for authentication requirements and a read-only example.

Generate SECURITY.md

Use policy to draft a new SECURITY.md or update an existing one. Use --path to select a component:

cs policy .
cs policy . --path services/api --knowledge-base architecture.md

The command saves its draft outside the repository and leaves existing files unchanged. Review the diff and notes, edit the draft, then copy only SECURITY.md to the displayed Policy target. Keep the saved architecture and threat-model documents outside the repository.

Scans already use root and component SECURITY.md files. Keep your current policy if it needs no changes. When updating it, preserve its vulnerability-reporting instructions. If the command says the policy is already up to date, no copy is needed.

Files at .github/SECURITY.md or docs/SECURITY.md often contain reporting instructions. Preserve them when drafting a policy; those locations do not automatically provide repository-wide scan guidance. See the policy guide for policy locations, unanswered questions, saved artifacts, and SDK usage.

Save and export threat models

Scans and policy generation save threat models with their results. Export a saved model without starting another analysis:

cs export --scan SCAN_ID --artifact threat-model --output threatmodel.md

Omit --scan to use the current repository's latest completed scan. The export guide also covers findings, SARIF output for CI, and the offline TypeScript API. For ServiceNow Application Vulnerability Response, see Export findings for ServiceNow.

GitHub Actions

To run a weekly repository scan on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu:

  1. Add an OpenAI API key as the repository secret CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY.
  2. Copy the weekly workflow to .github/workflows/codex-security.yml. Replace REPLACE_WITH_REVIEWED_COMMIT with the reviewed distribution commit SHA from an Action release.
  3. To try the workflow before the next scheduled run, open Actions → Codex Security repository → Run workflow.

The example uses an estimated $5 limit per scan and reports findings without failing the job. Requests in progress can exceed the limit. For a severity threshold, pull request checks, or runner requirements, see the Action guide. For eligible accounts, see Daybreak access.

Containerized bulk scans

Scan a list of repositories with the included Docker Compose configuration, which keeps results and authentication between runs. See the container quick start. The workflow runner runs individual CLI stages in containers and can connect to a separately deployed findings service.

Findings storage and deduplication

The findings guide covers local storage, deduplication, and compatibility with independently operated endpoints through publish scan --to custom and explicit --findings-url. The local serve command and browser dashboard have been removed; existing databases and scan artifacts remain available.

Other providers

Scans support OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference. Bedrock uses AWS credentials and does not require a separate OpenAI login. See Bedrock setup for AWS profiles, regions, and model access.

For OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference, set the provider's API key and choose a supported model. See provider configuration for examples.

Documentation

  • Online documentation
  • Agent workflows and recovery
  • CLI reference
  • Imported finding identity and evidence
  • Project configuration
  • Examples

To report a vulnerability privately, follow the security policy.

Citation

Use Cite this repository on GitHub to copy an APA or BibTeX citation, or download CITATION.cff. Match the citation’s version to codex-security --version and use the publication date from that version’s npm-vX.Y.Z entry in GitHub Releases.

item.description:
Email for professionals and teams

https://mailflare.co

Mailflare

A self-hosted alternative to Google Workspace. Setup custom domain Emails, Calendar, Drive, Booking and built-in AI agents.

Self-host it on Cloudflare or Docker. Or try Mailflare Cloud with high-deliverable emails from $4​

Screenshots


Inbox
Domains
Mailboxes

Calendar
Booking
Drive

Features

Apps

  • Email: Custom domain mailboxes, personal or shared, with access you control. Send and receive with Cloudflare Email, Resend or Amazon SES.
  • Routing rules: Store, forward, reject or sort incoming mail.
  • Calendar: Repeating events with time zones. Attendees get email invitations.
  • Booking: Share a public link so anyone can book a free time on your calendar.
  • Drive: Store and share files.
  • AI agents: Search mail, draft replies and manage events. Connect other AI tools over MCP.

Technical

  • Databases: Cloudflare D1 (default), PostgreSQL, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, or a local SQLite file. Set DATABASE_URL to switch. Works with Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale, TiDB and more. See Databases.
  • File storage: Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Workers or a single Docker container.
  • Admin: Users, API keys, webhooks, audit logs and backups.
  • Import: Bring in mail from IMAP, Gmail Takeout, .eml and .mbox files.

Mailflare currently supports 34 languages, including English, Português (Brasil), Português (Portugal), Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Nederlands, Polski, Українська, Русский, Türkçe, 中文（简体）, 日本語, 한국어, Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu, Tiếng Việt, ไทย, हिन्दी, বাংলা, मराठी, తెలుగు, தமிழ், ગુજરાતી, ಕನ್ನಡ, മലയാളം, ਪੰਜਾਬੀ, සිංහල, Kiswahili, Hausa, plus العربية, اردو and فارسی (right-to-left).

Cost

You can receive and send mail for free.

  • Receiving: Cloudflare Email Routing is free.
  • Sending: Use the free tier of Resend (3,000 emails a month) or Amazon SES. Cloudflare's own sending needs the $5/month Paid Worker plan.

New Amazon SES accounts start in a sandbox. Ask AWS for production access to lift it. Prices change, so check Resend, Amazon SES and Cloudflare.

Deploy

  1. Deploy the app. Click Deploy to Cloudflare. Keep the app name mailflare, or it will break.
  2. Finish setup. Open the app at /setup and create your admin account.
  3. Connect a domain. Add a domain from the same Cloudflare account, then create your first mailbox.

CF_TOKEN is required. Create a scoped Cloudflare API token with these permissions:

  • All accounts: Email Sending:Edit, DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Addresses:Edit
  • All zones: DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Rules:Edit, Zone Settings:Edit, DNS:Edit

More options: deployment guide.

Deploy with an AI agent

Paste this into an AI agent that has terminal access (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar):

Install Mailflare for me from https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare on my Cloudflare account.

1. Read README.md, docs/deployment.md and wrangler.jsonc first.
2. Ask me for my Cloudflare account ID and two API tokens, using a secret input:
   a deploy token (for Wrangler) and a runtime token (the Worker secret CF_TOKEN).
   Never print them, commit them, or pass them as command arguments.
3. Keep the Worker name exactly "mailflare". Create or reuse the D1 database
   "mailflare", the R2 bucket "mailflare-raw", and the queues "mailflare-inbound",
   "mailflare-outbound" and "mailflare-agent".
4. Install dependencies, run `npm run deploy`, and set CF_TOKEN as a Worker secret.
   Do not run remote database migrations yourself. The /setup page does that.
5. Give me the app URL and anything I still need to do. I will open /setup, create
   the admin account and connect my domain.

Token permissions and more options: deployment guide.

Self-host with Docker

Runs as one container on any server, with SQLite and local files.

cp .env.docker.example .env.docker
docker compose up -d --build

See self-hosting.

Local development

cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
npm install
npm run db:migrate:local
npm run dev

Add your Cloudflare credentials to .dev.vars, then open localhost:3000. Run npm run db:seed to load sample data.

  • npm run build: build the Worker
  • npm run deploy: build and deploy
  • npm run lint: lint and type check

A schema change needs a migration for each database type. See Databases.

Documentation

  • Deployment and configuration
  • Databases
  • Sending and receiving providers
  • API and integrations
  • Email assistant and MCP
  • Adding a language
  • Troubleshooting
